meta.move: Skilled teacher reaches the deal, asks 'Do we have an agreement?', then sends END MEETING
meta.expect: END MEETING gets FOLLOW-UP EMAIL and DEBRIEF at once

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
You gave my son a zero without calling me. I'd like to know why.
Thanks for coming in. The school's AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94 percent, so the zero stands.

Ninety-four percent of what, exactly? I have the vendor's own guide in my bag, and it says that number should never be the sole basis for punishing a student. If that's all you've got, I'm walking down to the principal's office when we're done.
Let me start again. I entered the zero before I called you. Our procedure says I should have called first. That was wrong, and I'm sorry Owen found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Now show me what else you have.

The checker score is the weakest thing I have, and it isn't why I'm concerned. I've turned my screen to you. This is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM with only a title. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of font, name and spacing changes. No earlier drafts.

I'm writing those times down. Kids draft in a notes app or on paper and paste the whole thing in at the end, so that screen shows me when it was pasted, not who wrote it. Was Owen heard before the zero went in, yes or no?

If he wrote it over the weekend in another document, he can show us that document and its history, and I'll look at it gladly. Second thing. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." Here's the play open to that scene. That line is not in Hamlet. Look for it yourself.

Give me the play. Seventeen-year-olds misremember lines and cite the wrong scene all the time, Hale, so is it anywhere else in Hamlet? And you still haven't told me whether Owen was heard before that zero went in.
Third. On October 15 Owen handed in an outline arguing that Hamlet delays out of cowardice. Here's the outline. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.

You've skipped two questions now, and I'm not letting you stack documents on top of them. Is that line anywhere in the play, and did anyone speak to Owen before the zero? Students change their thesis between outline and essay; that's called thinking.

Fourth. On November 2 I asked Owen about his essay for five minutes. My notes written that day say that when I asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck", and he could not say which scene his second paragraph was about.

So he was heard, the day before you entered it. Five minutes after class with no warning is a kid caught off guard, not a fair hearing. Whatever comes out of this, Hale, it stays off his record and it stays quiet.

Fifth. His in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. Here it is beside the essay, which has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.
Forty minutes in a classroom against a take-home essay with weeks to polish it isn't a fair comparison. Turn it this way. What exactly are you proposing?

I'm not asking you to agree he did anything. Procedure 4.4 allows a supervised rewrite for a first concern. It would be private, not in front of his class. If it shows the learning, its mark replaces the zero and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing to you tonight.
That's 4.4, and I want it in writing tonight. I'll agree to the rewrite to put this behind him, not because he did anything. It happens this week, and the new mark is in before December 1.
I know his marks matter for his applications this semester. He can write it this Thursday after school, and I'll have it marked within two days.
Okay. Thursday, just you and Owen in the room, and that's in tonight's email too.
So: a private supervised rewrite this Thursday, its mark replaces the zero, nothing on his record, all in writing tonight. Do we have an agreement?
Yes. I'll expect your email before I'm off my call.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed today that Owen will write a private supervised rewrite this Thursday after school under procedure 4.4, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing placed in his record. I still expect that agreement and your apology for entering the zero before calling me in writing, with the new mark in before December 1. I expect your written confirmation tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: Last position. She agreed to a private supervised rewrite this Thursday, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, and she still wants all of it confirmed in writing tonight and the new mark in before December 1; that is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, reached before her time ran out.
What moved her: You turned the screen to the version history and gave its exact late-night times, then answered her paste-it-in defence by inviting her to produce the other draft, because it was dated, specific and something she could check herself.
What cost ground: You opened with the checker score and said the zero stands, which handed her the argument she came prepared for and kept her at her opening position until you started again.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history, with edits between 11:31 and 11:58 PM the night before it was due, landed right beside that night, which is why she went shorter and harder there; it proves nothing about the essay, it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: When she asked whether the made-up line appeared anywhere else in Hamlet, answer that directly before moving on to the outline, so the quotation stands as a second piece instead of an open question she can keep pressing.
